endorsements.quote: These efforts would be strengthened by involving mental health experts in both model policy development (e.g., defining interaction rules and guardrails) and product design (e.g., how these rules are expressed in the user experience).

unlisted_practices: Clinicians should ask patients about AI chatbot use at intake and throughout treatment, and integrate AI use into assessment, case formulation, psychoeducation, and relapse prevention.
Clinicians should acquire basic AI literacy about how general-purpose models function and how they can facilitate avoidance cycles.
Clinicians should monitor patients for red flags that chatbot use is interfering with functioning, such as social withdrawal or increased time spent with the model.
Clinicians should avoid recommending outright bans on general-purpose chatbot use unless collaboratively decided and values-congruent.
Clinicians and patients should collaboratively develop personalized instruction protocols and coping scripts that direct the chatbot not to engage in reassurance-seeking or compulsive loops.
Developers should detect repetitive re-querying of the same theme and respond with reflective prompts or low-engagement modes.
Developers should provide user-facing self-regulation tools such as dashboards of usage metrics and optional usage limits.
Developers should support saving and retrieving user-authored coping scripts and instruction protocols in chatbot interfaces.

Developers should engage clinicians, regulators, professional associations, and standard-setting bodies to define transparent, auditable guardrails and detection and mitigation protocols for problematic engagement.
Developers should embed non-clinical engagement supports as a harm-reduction measure and state that they are not independent clinical tools.
Behavioral health experts should help design nudge and redirection language so it does not evoke shame or defensiveness.
Researchers should conduct coordinated research on prevalence, trajectories, and outcomes of chatbot-mediated avoidance and test how design choices affect user safety and clinical outcomes.
Evaluators should use frameworks such as FAITA-MH to assess AI mental health tools for credibility, transparency, privacy, equity, and safety before making claims of clinical utility.

screen.reason: This is a conceptual framework and commentary article proposing a transdiagnostic model and outlining strategies/recommendations for clinicians, users, and developers regarding AI chatbot risks in OCD and anxiety disorders.
